More than 1,300 people are missing in Nepal and Tibet, including 47 Americans, after a glacial collapse caused catastrophic floods, with video showing mud sweeping through entire communities. Drone footage in Nepal showed roads destroyed and buildings buried by thundering water the color of wet cement. Nepalese authorities ramped up operations in the worst-affected districts of Nuwakot and Rasuwa. The disaster in Nepal and Tibet is not a one-off. The Lhende Khola river system has now flooded twice in just 14 months and the increasingly unstable Himalayan ice system threatens communities, infrastructure and water supplies across one of the world’s most densely populated regions. The region saw similar flash floods in August last year, when a glacial lake in Tibet overflowed because of high temperatures. Nine people were killed, and critical infrastructure, including a bridge connecting Nepal and China, was damaged.

Scientists have said it is too early to draw a direct connection between global warming and Wednesday’s catastrophe. However, they said that as Earth’s temperature rose due to human activities such as burning oil, gas, and coal, the likelihood of such disasters increased, especially in the Himalayan mountains, which were warming considerably faster than many other parts of the world. #Himalayan #Flood #Nepal #Share #FY

Two people have been rescued from a hydropower tunnel in Nepal, a dramatic breakthrough more than a week after catastrophic floods hit the country’s border with China. CNN's Hanako Montgomery reports.

The office of Nepal's energy minister says two people have been rescued alive from a hydropower tunnel nine days after floods hit the area. Earlier on Friday, Energy Minister Biraj Bhakta Shrestha's office said in a statement the two workers pulled from the tunnel at the Upper Trishuli 3A Hydropower Station are Sanjay Sah, a mechanical foreman, and Kabir Maharjan, a mechanical supervisor. Mr Maharjan cannot move his hands and legs but Mr Sah's injuries are not critical, an aide to the energy minister told Reuters news agency. The two are being taken to a hospital in Kathmandu, he said. The rescues come nine days after the August 26 floods, likely caused by a glacier collapse, that devastated towns and valleys in Nepal. At least 1,259 people were killed and more than 5,000 remain missing, according to the country's disaster management agency. China, as of late Wednesday, said 21 people were killed and 541 were missing on the Tibet side of the border. About 900 workers are missing from 12 hydropower projects in Nepal, with roughly 500 believed to be trapped in tunnels, according to local authorities. #Nepal #ABCNews

The 2026 Nepal Flood Explained: Where Did All The Water Come From? (Part 1) On August 26, 2026, a catastrophic flash flood struck the Nepal-Tibet border, erasing infrastructure in a terrifying 13-minute window. Initial global reports blamed a simple earthquake or a glacial lake outburst—but satellite imagery and seismic data proved both theories completely wrong. In Part 1 of this forensic scientific investigation, we solve the central mystery: Where did millions of cubic meters of water suddenly originate in a valley with no lake? Nepal has been hit by a catastrophic flash flood disaster, beginning on 26 August 2026, particularly along the Bhote Koshi and Trishuli river corridors. 🇳🇵 What happened? The flooding was not simply ordinary monsoon flooding. A sudden ice/rock avalanche and collapse in the Himalayan region near Tibet caused a huge surge of water, mud, rocks and debris into the Bhote Koshi River. The resulting flash flood swept through villages and infrastructure with very little warning.  The worst-affected areas include Rasuwa, Nuwakot, Dhading and Chitwan, with impacts also reported in Gorkha and Tanahun.  🕯️ Deaths and missing people The situation has continued to worsen as rescue teams recover bodies and update missing-person lists. As of 29–30 August, reports indicate more than 600 people have died in Nepal, with thousands still missing across Nepal and Tibet. AP reported 669 deaths in Nepal and nearly 3,000 people still missing as of August 30.  Many of the missing include foreign nationals, tourists, pilgrims and workers. 🚨 Rescue operation Nepalese security forces, helicopters and emergency teams are continuing search-and-rescue operations. More than 3,700 people have reportedly been rescued, while difficult mountain terrain, damaged roads and unstable conditions are making the operation extremely difficult.  A temporary lake formed near the disaster area also created fears of another flood, although the immediate risk has reportedly decreased as the lake has begun draining.  💔 Damage The floods have destroyed or severely damaged: Homes and entire villages Roads and bridges Hydropower plants Electricity infrastructure Border/trade infrastructure Health facilities Tourist and pilgrimage routes Nepal's government estimates that rebuilding could cost approximately US$4–5 billion.  The Nepal Ministry of Foreign Affairs has also been publishing official updates on the disaster and missing foreign nationals.  Important: Some dramatic videos circulating on Sri Lankan social media claiming to show the Nepal floods are actually old or unrelated footage, so they should not automatically be trusted. videos.caption: Two workers have been pulled alive from a hydropower tunnel nine days after the devastating floods in Nepal as emergency teams continued to search for hundreds of others believed to be trapped inside. Officials identified the two men as a mechanical foreman and a mechanical supervisor. At least 557 workers are missing from the Trishuli 3A hydropower project along the Trishuli River, with about 115 believed to be trapped in the main tunnel, according to the Independent Power Producers Association of Nepal. Rescuers believe some people may still be alive inside the tunnel. #nepal  #flood
